```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern discriminated-union
 * @options e15c08293d2387fd
 */

/**
 * The order exists and has been costed.
 *
 * The discriminant is a literal type rather than a `string`, which is the whole
 * mechanism. `kind: string` would compile everywhere this does and narrow
 * nowhere, leaving every branch in every consumer looking at the union — an
 * ordinary interface with one field nobody can use.
 */
export interface OrderPlaced {
  readonly kind: "placed";
  readonly id: string;
  readonly total: number;
}

/**
 * It has left, and something outside now has custody of it.
 */
export interface OrderShipped {
  readonly kind: "shipped";
  readonly id: string;
  readonly carrier: string;
}

/**
 * It will not happen, and the reason is part of the record rather than a log
 * line.
 */
export interface OrderCancelled {
  readonly kind: "cancelled";
  readonly id: string;
  readonly reason: string;
}

/**
 * Exactly one of the shapes above — never two, and never a blend of them.
 *
 * The alternative most codebases reach for first is one interface with optional
 * fields: `{ kind: string; total?: number; carrier?: string }`. It costs
 * nothing to write and it makes every illegal combination representable —
 * shipped with a cancellation reason, placed with no total — so every reader
 * downstream has to decide what those mean, and each decides differently. The
 * union removes the question by removing the states.
 */
export type OrderEvent = OrderPlaced | OrderShipped | OrderCancelled;

/**
 * Every discriminant value, derived rather than restated.
 *
 * Written out by hand it would be a second list to keep in step with the first,
 * and the failure is silent: a member added to the union and forgotten here
 * leaves a name for something the type no longer describes.
 */
export type OrderEventKind = OrderEvent["kind"];

/**
 * Records that the order exists and has been costed.
 *
 * The declared return type is doing work. Without it the inferred `kind` widens
 * to `string`, and a value built here would not be assignable to the union — or
 * worse, in a wider context, would be assignable and then narrow to nothing.
 */
export function placed(id: string, total: number): OrderPlaced {
  return { kind: "placed", id, total };
}

/**
 * Records that it has left, and who has custody of it.
 */
export function shipped(id: string, carrier: string): OrderShipped {
  return { kind: "shipped", id, carrier };
}

/**
 * Records that it will not happen, and why.
 */
export function cancelled(id: string, reason: string): OrderCancelled {
  return { kind: "cancelled", id, reason };
}

/**
 * Whether an event is OrderPlaced.
 *
 * Explicit rather than inferred, for a reason that is easy to miss. The
 * compiler will infer a predicate from an unannotated body that does nothing
 * but narrow, so `filter((event) => event.kind === "placed")` narrows on its
 * own — but annotating that function `: boolean`, which an explicit-return-type
 * lint rule requires, opts out silently and leaves the elements as the full
 * union. Stating the predicate satisfies both, and can be passed by name.
 */
export function isOrderPlaced(event: OrderEvent): event is OrderPlaced {
  return event.kind === "placed";
}

/**
 * Whether an event is OrderShipped.
 */
export function isOrderShipped(event: OrderEvent): event is OrderShipped {
  return event.kind === "shipped";
}

/**
 * Whether an event is OrderCancelled.
 */
export function isOrderCancelled(event: OrderEvent): event is OrderCancelled {
  return event.kind === "cancelled";
}

/**
 * A discriminant nobody declared.
 *
 * Unreachable from typed code, and reachable from everywhere else: a value
 * parsed from JSON, a message from an older producer, a caller who is not using
 * TypeScript at all. The types stop at the module boundary and the data does
 * not, so the case that "cannot happen" gets a name and a value attached rather
 * than a crash somewhere further on.
 */
export class UnknownOrderEventError extends Error {
  readonly received: unknown;

  constructor(received: unknown) {
    super(`unhandled OrderEvent: ${JSON.stringify(received)}`);
    this.name = "UnknownOrderEventError";
    this.received = received;
  }
}

/**
 * Establishes that every case has been handled.
 *
 * The parameter is `never`, so this is callable only where the compiler has
 * narrowed the value away to nothing. Add a member to the union and every
 * `switch` that reaches here stops compiling, naming the member it does not
 * handle — which is the entire reason the default branch is not simply a thrown
 * error.
 *
 * It throws as well, because the compiler's proof covers typed callers only.
 */
export function assertNever(value: never): never {
  throw new UnknownOrderEventError(value);
}

/**
 * One answer per case.
 *
 * The default branch is not error handling. It is where the compiler is asked
 * to confirm nothing is left, and it is the only part of this function that has
 * to be remembered — which is the honest weakness of the flow-based form, since
 * a `switch` written without it compiles perfectly well and silently returns
 * `undefined` for a member added later.
 */
export function summarise(event: OrderEvent): string {
  switch (event.kind) {
    case "placed":
      return `${event.id} placed (${String(event.total)})`;
    case "shipped":
      return `${event.id} shipped (${event.carrier})`;
    case "cancelled":
      return `${event.id} cancelled (${event.reason})`;
    default:
      return assertNever(event);
  }
}
```

## order-event-example.ts (example)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern discriminated-union
 * @options e15c08293d2387fd
 */

/**
 * Using the union, and the mistakes it refuses.
 *
 * The refusals at the end are assertions rather than a demonstration: each
 * `@ts-expect-error` states that the line under it must *not* compile. The
 * guarantee this pattern exists for is that a case cannot be quietly left out,
 * and a guarantee nothing asserts is a hope — so it is pinned here, in a file
 * emitted whether or not the caller wanted tests.
 */

import {
  assertNever,
  cancelled,
  isOrderShipped,
  placed,
  shipped,
} from "./order-event.js";
import type { OrderEvent, OrderEventKind, OrderPlaced } from "./order-event.js";

/**
 * A history, built through the constructors.
 *
 * The annotation is load-bearing rather than decorative. Each constructor
 * declares its return type, so `kind` stays a literal and these values belong
 * to the union; were those annotations dropped, `kind` would be inferred as
 * `string` and this array — which looks like the most ordinary line in the file
 * — would stop compiling.
 */
export const history: readonly OrderEvent[] = [
  placed("A-1", 2500),
  shipped("A-1", "royal-mail"),
  cancelled("A-1", "out-of-stock"),
];

/**
 * A second consumer, written the same way as the first.
 *
 * Every consumer needs its own default branch. That is the cost of the
 * flow-based form — the guarantee is per function, and a function written
 * without one still compiles.
 */
export function notify(event: OrderEvent): string {
  switch (event.kind) {
    case "placed":
      return `invoice ${event.id} for ${String(event.total)}`;
    case "shipped":
      return `tracking for ${event.id} via ${event.carrier}`;
    case "cancelled":
      return `refund ${event.id}: ${event.reason}`;
    default:
      return assertNever(event);
  }
}

/**
 * Narrowing outside a dispatch.
 *
 * Passing the predicate by name is what narrows the result to `readonly
 * OrderShipped[]`. An inline arrow would also narrow, since the compiler infers
 * a predicate from a body that only narrows — but a named helper annotated `:
 * boolean` would not, and that annotation is exactly what an
 * explicit-return-type lint rule asks for.
 */
export function carriers(events: readonly OrderEvent[]): readonly string[] {
  return events.filter(isOrderShipped).map((event) => event.carrier);
}

/**
 * Counting by case.
 *
 * A second place completeness is enforced structurally, and it works in either
 * dispatch style: `Record<OrderEventKind, number>` requires every key, so the
 * initialiser cannot omit a case and cannot invent one. Add a member to the
 * union and this stops compiling too.
 */
export function tally(
  events: readonly OrderEvent[],
): Record<OrderEventKind, number> {
  const counts: Record<OrderEventKind, number> = {
    placed: 0,
    shipped: 0,
    cancelled: 0,
  };

  for (const event of events) {
    counts[event.kind] += 1;
  }

  return counts;
}

/**
 * Folding a history into a state.
 *
 * The reason to model events this way rather than mutating a record: the state
 * is a function of the events, so it can be recomputed, and a state that was
 * never reachable through these transitions cannot be represented.
 */
export function outcome(
  events: readonly OrderEvent[],
): "open" | "shipped" | "cancelled" {
  return events.reduce<"open" | "shipped" | "cancelled">((state, event) => {
    if (event.kind === "shipped") return "shipped";
    if (event.kind === "cancelled") return "cancelled";

    return state;
  }, "open");
}

/**
 * The refusals, asserted.
 *
 * `@ts-expect-error` inverts the usual reading: it is satisfied by an error and
 * violated by silence. Each directive sits alone on its line with the reason
 * above it, because a directive only governs the line it begins on and a long
 * comment gets re-wrapped.
 *
 * Where the error is a property of an object, the directive sits inside the
 * object, on the line above that property. Above the whole statement it would
 * break for a long enough type name: the literal then wraps, the error is
 * reported against the property's own line, and the directive governs only the
 * `const` — so the assertion silently inverts into two errors, one for the
 * escaped mistake and one for a directive with nothing left to suppress. A
 * comment inside a literal also stops the formatter collapsing it, so the shape
 * does not depend on the name.
 */

export function refusesAnIncompleteSwitch(event: OrderEvent): string {
  switch (event.kind) {
    case "placed":
      return event.id;
    case "shipped":
      return event.id;
    default:
      // "cancelled" has not been handled, so the value is not `never` here.
      // @ts-expect-error
      return assertNever(event);
  }
}

export function refusesABlendedValue(): void {
  // "placed" carries a total and not a carrier. In one interface with optional
  // fields this would be an ordinary value, and every reader would have to
  // decide what it meant.
  const bad: OrderPlaced = {
    kind: "placed",
    id: "A-1",
    // @ts-expect-error
    carrier: "royal-mail",
  };

  void bad;
}

export function refusesTheWrongField(event: OrderEvent): void {
  if (event.kind === "placed") {
    // Narrowed to OrderPlaced, which has no carrier.
    // @ts-expect-error
    const bad: string = event.carrier;

    void bad;
  }
}

export function refusesAnUndeclaredKind(): void {
  // The set of cases is closed. A discriminant nobody declared is not a member
  // of the union, which is why the run-time check for one exists only for
  // values arriving from outside the type system.
  const bad: OrderEvent = {
    // @ts-expect-error
    kind: "refunded",
    id: "A-1",
    total: 2500,
  };

  void bad;
}
```

## order-event.test-d.ts (test)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern discriminated-union
 * @options e15c08293d2387fd
 */

/**
 * What the compiler is asked to prove.
 *
 * Nothing here runs, and nothing should: the suffix keeps this file out of
 * every runner while leaving it in front of the compiler, which is the only
 * thing that can check a claim about a type. A union that had stopped
 * discriminating would behave identically at run time to one that still did.
 *
 * No claim below concerns nullability. With `strictNullChecks` off `undefined`
 * is assignable to everything, so such a claim would mean one thing for one
 * caller and the opposite for another.
 */

import { isOrderShipped, placed } from "./order-event.js";
import type {
  OrderEvent,
  OrderEventKind,
  OrderPlaced,
  OrderShipped,
} from "./order-event.js";

/**
 * Forces its argument to be `true`, and fails to compile when it is not.
 *
 * Each assertion below is written as a named alias rather than a bare one, so
 * that it reads as a stated claim about the code and cannot be mistaken for a
 * leftover.
 */
export type Expect<T extends true> = T;

/**
 * Whether two types are identical, rather than merely assignable in both
 * directions.
 *
 * The two-function form looks like a trick because it is one: it compares the
 * types in a position the compiler checks by identity instead of by
 * assignability. The obvious alternative — asking whether each extends the
 * other — answers a different question, and answers it wrongly in two common
 * cases. It reports `true` for `any` against anything at all, and it
 * distributes over unions, so a union compared against one of its own members
 * can come back true.
 */
export type Equal<X, Y> =
  (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends <T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2
    ? true
    : false;

/**
 * Whether `X` is assignable to `Y`.
 *
 * Both sides are wrapped in a tuple to stop the union distribution a bare
 * conditional performs. Undistributed is the question that was meant: whether
 * the whole of `X` is acceptable as a `Y`, rather than whether each member of
 * it is on its own.
 */
export type Extends<X, Y> = [X] extends [Y] ? true : false;

/**
 * Whether `X` is rejected where a `Y` is wanted.
 *
 * The type-level counterpart to `@ts-expect-error`, and preferable wherever the
 * claim is about a relationship rather than about a particular line: a
 * directive suppresses whichever error occurs, so it can be satisfied by an
 * unrelated mistake on the same line, where this cannot.
 */
export type NotAssignable<X, Y> = [X] extends [Y] ? false : true;

/**
 * The discriminant's values are exactly the tags, derived from the union rather
 * than restated.
 *
 * This is the claim that keeps the two lists in step: a member added to the
 * union widens `OrderEventKind` with no edit, and if it ever stopped doing so,
 * nothing would report the omission.
 */
export type KindsAreTheTags = Expect<
  Equal<OrderEventKind, "placed" | "shipped" | "cancelled">
>;

/**
 * Narrowing by the discriminant yields the member exactly, not something
 * assignable to it.
 */
export type ExtractIsExact = Expect<
  Equal<Extract<OrderEvent, { kind: "shipped" }>, OrderShipped>
>;

/**
 * A member is not the union.
 *
 * The direction that matters: a function taking one case cannot be handed the
 * whole union by accident, which is what makes the narrowing in a dispatch
 * worth anything.
 */
export type UnionIsNotAMember = Expect<NotAssignable<OrderEvent, OrderPlaced>>;
export type MemberIsTheUnion = Expect<Extends<OrderPlaced, OrderEvent>>;

/**
 * The constructor pins the literal, rather than widening it.
 *
 * Without the declared return type the inferred `kind` would be `string`, and
 * this claim is the one that notices — the value would still build, still run,
 * and narrow nowhere.
 */
export type ConstructorKeepsTheLiteral = Expect<
  Equal<ReturnType<typeof placed>, OrderPlaced>
>;

/**
 * The predicate narrows an array, which is the case it exists for.
 *
 * Worth stating because the alternative nearly works: an inline arrow narrows
 * too, through an inferred predicate, and the moment that arrow is extracted
 * into a helper annotated `: boolean` the narrowing disappears with no
 * diagnostic anywhere.
 */
export function shippedOnly(
  events: readonly OrderEvent[],
): readonly OrderShipped[] {
  return events.filter(isOrderShipped);
}

export type PredicateNarrowsAnArray = Expect<
  Equal<ReturnType<typeof shippedOnly>, readonly OrderShipped[]>
>;
```

## order-event.test.ts (test)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern discriminated-union
 * @options e15c08293d2387fd
 */

/**
 * What is left for a suite that runs.
 *
 * Not exhaustiveness — that is settled before this file executes, and
 * `order-event.test-d.ts` is where it is asserted. What remains is what the
 * types do not decide: the answer each case produces, and the one case typed
 * code cannot reach — a value from outside carrying a discriminant nobody
 * declared, which is the only reason the run-time check exists at all.
 */

import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";

import {
  UnknownOrderEventError,
  cancelled,
  isOrderCancelled,
  isOrderPlaced,
  isOrderShipped,
  placed,
  shipped,
  summarise,
} from "./order-event.js";
import type { OrderEvent } from "./order-event.js";

describe("summarise", () => {
  // A table rather than three cases, so that a member added to the union and
  // left out of the table is visible as a missing row next to the others.
  const cases: readonly { event: OrderEvent; expected: string }[] = [
    { event: placed("A-1", 2500), expected: "A-1 placed (2500)" },
    {
      event: shipped("A-1", "royal-mail"),
      expected: "A-1 shipped (royal-mail)",
    },
    {
      event: cancelled("A-1", "out-of-stock"),
      expected: "A-1 cancelled (out-of-stock)",
    },
  ];

  it("answers for every case", () => {
    expect(cases).toHaveLength(3);

    for (const { event, expected } of cases) {
      expect(summarise(event)).toBe(expected);
    }
  });
});

describe("the predicates", () => {
  const history: readonly OrderEvent[] = [
    placed("A-1", 2500),
    shipped("A-1", "royal-mail"),
    cancelled("A-2", "out-of-stock"),
  ];

  it("each admits its own case and no other", () => {
    expect(history.filter(isOrderPlaced)).toHaveLength(1);
    expect(history.filter(isOrderShipped)).toHaveLength(1);
    expect(history.filter(isOrderCancelled)).toHaveLength(1);
  });

  it("partition the history exactly", () => {
    // Every event belongs to one predicate and one only. Overlapping predicates
    // would make a filtered list narrower than its contents, which no type
    // would report.
    const counted =
      history.filter(isOrderPlaced).length +
      history.filter(isOrderShipped).length +
      history.filter(isOrderCancelled).length;

    expect(counted).toBe(history.length);
  });
});

describe("a value from outside the type system", () => {
  // Constructed through `unknown` rather than with a cast to the union, because
  // that is how it actually arrives: parsed from JSON, or handed over by a
  // caller not using TypeScript. A cast would be asserting the very thing under
  // test.
  const outside = JSON.parse('{"kind":"refunded","id":"A-9"}') as OrderEvent;

  it("is reported with the value that caused it", () => {
    // Matched on the message rather than the class, because the next case
    // establishes the class and this one is about what a reader is told: the
    // union that failed to match, not `undefined is not a function`.
    expect(() => summarise(outside)).toThrow(/unhandled OrderEvent/);
  });

  it("names the union and the value, not the mechanism", () => {
    // A `TypeError` about calling undefined, or about reading a property of
    // undefined, would be true and useless. What a reader needs is which value
    // failed and what it failed to match.
    let caught: unknown;
    try {
      summarise(outside);
    } catch (error) {
      caught = error;
    }

    expect(caught instanceof UnknownOrderEventError).toBe(true);
    expect((caught as UnknownOrderEventError).received).toEqual(outside);
  });
});
```
